text:
The three days of travel in Genesis 22 may be read as a kind of suspended sentence. Nothing outward happens in them, and yet everything of consequence is decided. The narrator dwells on the servants, the wood, the knife, and the fire; and by dwelling on them he names the instruments of the act before the act itself is come. Obedience and horror are both present in every verse, and neither is suffered to prevail over the other. Faith, as the narrator conceives it, is an ordering of persons and things, a fixed relation among them, and has little in it of feeling.

When the scene is compared with the earlier promise, the difference between them grows smaller than it first appears. The reader is reminded that Isaac is the child of the covenant, the son through whom the nations are to be blessed; and it is that very promise which the narrator converts into a test. The whole scene turns upon a single word, _hineni_, "here I am," which Abraham speaks three times: to God, to Isaac, and to the angel. Each time the word means something different, and each time it costs him more. The word by which Abraham declares himself present is the word by which he consents to lose his son.
